The city where Euclid—often called the “father of geometry”—lived and worked is **Alexandria**.  
Alexandria was founded by **Alexander the Great** (356 – 323 BCE) in 331 BCE.  

> *“Alexandria was founded by Alexander the Great in April 331 BC …”* (Wikipedia: *Alexandria*)  

Thus, the founder of the city in which the founder of geometry lived is Alexander the Great.

So the city is Alexandria, founded by Alexander the Great. So the answer: Alexander the Great. Alternatively maybe "Pythagoras" founder of geometry? But Pythagoras was founder of geometry? Actually Euclid is known as the father of geometry. So answer: Alexander the Great.

**Euclid** (; Ancient Greek: Εὐκλείδης; fl.300 BC) was an ancient Greek mathematician active as a geometer and logician.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBruno2003[httpsarchiveorgdetailsmathmathematicia00brunpage125_125]-2) Considered the "father of geometry",[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-FOOTNOTESialaros2021%C2%A7_%22Summary%22-3) he is chiefly known for the _[Elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's\_Elements "Euclid's Elements")_ treatise, which established the foundations of geometry that largely dominated the field until the early 19th century. His system, now referred to as Euclidean geometry, involved innovations in combination with a synthesis of theories from earlier Greek mathematicians, including Eudoxus of Cnidus, Hippocrates of Chios, Thales and Theaetetus. With Archimedes and Apollonius of Perga, Euclid is generally considered among the greatest mathematicians of antiquity, and one of the most influential in the history of mathematics.

Very little is known of Euclid's life, and most information comes from the scholars Proclus and Pappus of Alexandria many centuries later. Medieval Islamic mathematicians invented a fanciful biography, and medieval Byzantine and early Renaissance scholars mistook him for the earlier philosopher Euclid of Megara. It is now generally accepted that he spent his career in Alexandria and lived around 300 BC, after Plato's students and before Archimedes. There is some speculation that Euclid studied at the Platonic Academy and later taught at the Musaeum; he is regarded as bridging the earlier Platonic tradition in Athens with the later tradition of Alexandria.
In the _Elements_, Euclid deduced the theorems from a small set of axioms. He also wrote works on perspective, conic sections, spherical geometry, number theory, and mathematical rigour. In addition to the _Elements_, Euclid wrote a central early text in the optics field, _[Optics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's\_Optics "Euclid's Optics")_, and lesser-known works including _[Data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's\_Data "Euclid's Data")_ and _Phaenomena_. Euclid's authorship of _On Divisions of Figures_ and _Catoptrics_ has been questioned. He is thought to have written many lost works.

## Life
### Traditional narrative
[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:0_Chambre_de_Rapha%C3%ABl_-_%C3%89cole_d'Ath%C3%A8nes_-_Mus%C3%A9es_du_Vatican.JPG)
Detail of Raphael's impression of Euclid, teaching students in _The School of Athens_ (1509–1511)
The English name 'Euclid' is the anglicized version of the Ancient Greek name _Eukleídes_ (Εὐκλείδης).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-FOOTNOTESialaros2021%C2%A7_%22Life%22-4)[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-6) It is derived from 'eu-' (εὖ; 'well'), 'klês' (-κλῆς; 'fame'), meaning "renowned, glorious",[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''OED''b-7) and the suffix '-ides' (-ίδης, 'son of'). In English, by metonymy, 'Euclid' can mean his most well-known work, [Euclid's _Elements_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's_Elements "Euclid's Elements"), or a copy thereof,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''OED''a-5) and is sometimes synonymous with 'geometry'.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBruno2003[httpsarchiveorgdetailsmathmathematicia00brunpage125_125]-2)

## Life
### Traditional narrative
As with many ancient Greek mathematicians, the details of Euclid's life are mostly unknown.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHeath1981354-8) He is accepted as the author of four mostly extant treatises—the _Elements_, _[Optics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's\_Optics "Euclid's Optics")_, _[Data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's\_Data "Euclid's Data")_, _[Phaenomena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's\_Phaenomena "Euclid's Phaenomena")_—but besides this, there is nothing known for certain of him.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAsper2010%C2%A7_para._1-9)[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-11) The traditional narrative mainly follows the 5th century AD account by Proclus in his _Commentary on the First Book of Euclid's Elements_, as well as a few anecdotes from Pappus of Alexandria in the early 4th century.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-FOOTNOTESialaros2021%C2%A7_%22Life%22-4)[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-13)

## Life

According to Proclus, Euclid lived shortly after several of Plato's (d.347 BC) followers and before the mathematician Archimedes (c.287– c.212 BC);[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-14) specifically, Proclus placed Euclid during the rule of Ptolemy I (r.305/304–282 BC).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHeath1981354-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAsper2010%C2%A7_para._1-9)[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-15) Euclid's birthdate is unknown;

# Euclid of Alexandria: Mathematician & Author of Elements
### Lawrence Jean-Louis
Published Oct 16, 2023
+ Follow
Following up on last week’s post, “Vitruvius: Roman Architect, Author and Engineer” today’s LinkedIn newsletter features Euclid, the Greek mathematician, who lived and taught in Alexandria during the reign of Ptolemy I. He's often referred to as the “Father of Geometry.”
“Not much younger than these [pupils of Plato] is Euclid, who put together the "Elements", arranging in order many of Eudoxus's theorems, perfecting many of Theaetetus's, and also bringing to irrefutable demonstration the things which had been only loosely proved by his predecessors. This man lived in the time of the first Ptolemy; for Archimedes, who followed closely upon the first Ptolemy makes mention of Euclid[…]. He is therefore younger than Plato's circle, but older than Eratosthenes and Archimedes; for these were contemporaries[…].”
---
Euclid of Alexandria, referred to as such to differentiate him from the earlier philosopher Euclid of Megara, a pupil of Socrates, is generally considered among the greatest mathematicians of antiquity, and one of the most influential in the history of mathematics.
He is accepted as the author of four treatises— Elements, Optics, which examines the mathematical theory of mirrors, especially images formed by plane and spherical concave mirrors, Data, a work on geometrical problems, and Phaenomena, which examines the mathematical theory of mirrors, especially images formed by plane and spherical concave mirrors
His 13-book treatise, Elements curates work from earlier mathematicians, including Pythagoras, Eudoxus, Hippocrates of Kos, Thales and Theaetetus, while other theorems are mentioned by Plato and Aristotle.
While Euclid did not originate most of the ideas in Elements, he:

# Euclid of Alexandria: Mathematician & Author of Elements
### Lawrence Jean-Louis
*   collected important mathematical and geometric knowledge in one book.

**Euclid** (; Ancient Greek: Εὐκλείδης; fl.300 BC) was an ancient Greek mathematician active as a geometer and logician.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBruno2003[httpsarchiveorgdetailsmathmathematicia00brunpage125_125]-2) Considered the "father of geometry",[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-FOOTNOTESialaros2021%C2%A7_%22Summary%22-3) he is chiefly known for the _[Elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's\_Elements "Euclid's Elements")_ treatise, which established the foundations of geometry that largely dominated the field until the early 19th century. His system, now referred to as Euclidean geometry, involved innovations in combination with a synthesis of theories from earlier Greek mathematicians, including Eudoxus of Cnidus, Hippocrates of Chios, Thales and Theaetetus. With Archimedes and Apollonius of Perga, Euclid is generally considered among the greatest mathematicians of antiquity, and one of the most influential in the history of mathematics.

Very little is known of Euclid's life, and most information comes from the scholars Proclus and Pappus of Alexandria many centuries later. Medieval Islamic mathematicians invented a fanciful biography, and medieval Byzantine and early Renaissance scholars mistook him for the earlier philosopher Euclid of Megara. It is now generally accepted that he spent his career in Alexandria and lived around 300 BC, after Plato's students and before Archimedes. There is some speculation that Euclid studied at the Platonic Academy and later taught at the Musaeum; he is regarded as bridging the earlier Platonic tradition in Athens with the later tradition of Alexandria.
In the _Elements_, Euclid deduced the theorems from a small set of axioms. He also wrote works on perspective, conic sections, spherical geometry, number theory, and mathematical rigour. In addition to the _Elements_, Euclid wrote a central early text in the optics field, _[Optics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's\_Optics "Euclid's Optics")_, and lesser-known works including _[Data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's\_Data "Euclid's Data")_ and _Phaenomena_. Euclid's authorship of _On Divisions of Figures_ and _Catoptrics_ has been questioned. He is thought to have written many lost works.

**Euclid** (; Ancient Greek: Εὐκλείδης; fl.300 BC) was an ancient Greek mathematician active as a geometer and logician.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBruno2003[httpsarchiveorgdetailsmathmathematicia00brunpage125_125]-2) Considered the "father of geometry",[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-FOOTNOTESialaros2021%C2%A7_%22Summary%22-3) he is chiefly known for the _[Elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's\_Elements "Euclid's Elements")_ treatise, which established the foundations of geometry that largely dominated the field until the early 19th century. His system, now referred to as Euclidean geometry, involved innovations in combination with a synthesis of theories from earlier Greek mathematicians, including Eudoxus of Cnidus, Hippocrates of Chios, Thales and Theaetetus. With Archimedes and Apollonius of Perga, Euclid is generally considered among the greatest mathematicians of antiquity, and one of the most influential in the history of mathematics.

Very little is known of Euclid's life, and most information comes from the scholars Proclus and Pappus of Alexandria many centuries later. Medieval Islamic mathematicians invented a fanciful biography, and medieval Byzantine and early Renaissance scholars mistook him for the earlier philosopher Euclid of Megara. It is now generally accepted that he spent his career in Alexandria and lived around 300 BC, after Plato's students and before Archimedes. There is some speculation that Euclid studied at the Platonic Academy and later taught at the Musaeum; he is regarded as bridging the earlier Platonic tradition in Athens with the later tradition of Alexandria.
In the _Elements_, Euclid deduced the theorems from a small set of axioms. He also wrote works on perspective, conic sections, spherical geometry, number theory, and mathematical rigour. In addition to the _Elements_, Euclid wrote a central early text in the optics field, _[Optics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's\_Optics "Euclid's Optics")_, and lesser-known works including _[Data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's\_Data "Euclid's Data")_ and _Phaenomena_. Euclid's authorship of _On Divisions of Figures_ and _Catoptrics_ has been questioned. He is thought to have written many lost works.

In English, by metonymy, 'Euclid' can mean his most well-known work, [Euclid's _Elements_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's_Elements "Euclid's Elements"), or a copy thereof,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''OED''a-5) and is sometimes synonymous with 'geometry'.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBruno2003[httpsarchiveorgdetailsmathmathematicia00brunpage125_125]-2)

Following up on last week’s post, “Vitruvius: Roman Architect, Author and Engineer” today’s LinkedIn newsletter features Euclid, the Greek mathematician, who lived and taught in Alexandria during the reign of Ptolemy I. He's often referred to as the “Father of Geometry.”
“Not much younger than these [pupils of Plato] is Euclid, who put together the "Elements", arranging in order many of Eudoxus's theorems, perfecting many of Theaetetus's, and also bringing to irrefutable demonstration the things which had been only loosely proved by his predecessors. This man lived in the time of the first Ptolemy; for Archimedes, who followed closely upon the first Ptolemy makes mention of Euclid[…]. He is therefore younger than Plato's circle, but older than Eratosthenes and Archimedes; for these were contemporaries[…].”
---
Euclid of Alexandria, referred to as such to differentiate him from the earlier philosopher Euclid of Megara, a pupil of Socrates, is generally considered among the greatest mathematicians of antiquity, and one of the most influential in the history of mathematics.
He is accepted as the author of four treatises— Elements, Optics, which examines the mathematical theory of mirrors, especially images formed by plane and spherical concave mirrors, Data, a work on geometrical problems, and Phaenomena, which examines the mathematical theory of mirrors, especially images formed by plane and spherical concave mirrors
His 13-book treatise, Elements curates work from earlier mathematicians, including Pythagoras, Eudoxus, Hippocrates of Kos, Thales and Theaetetus, while other theorems are mentioned by Plato and Aristotle.
While Euclid did not originate most of the ideas in Elements, he:

*   collected important mathematical and geometric knowledge in one book.  
*   gave definitions, postulates, and axioms, which he called "common notions."  
*   presented geometry as an axiomatic system: Every statement was either an axiom, a postulate, or was proven by clear logical steps from axioms and postulates.  
*   gave some of his own original discoveries, such as the first known proof that there are infinitely many prime numbers.
Besides this, there is nothing known for certain of him except that he taught at Alexandria in Egypt and no likeness or first-hand description of his physical appearance has survived.

Euclid's date of death is also unknown; it has been speculated that he died c. 270 BC.
The Elements remained the definitive textbook on geometry and mathematics for well over two millennia and through Arabic translations.
Persian mathematician, astronomer, astrologer geographer and a scholar in the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, was likely familiar with Euclid's Elements. During Harun al-Rashid's reign, al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, one of al-Khwarizmi's colleagues, had translated Euclid's Elements into Arabic.
Many forms of mathematics are named after Euclid, including Euclidean Geometry, Euclidean Number and Euclidean Algorithm.

One of the best biographies of Alexander, with great attention paid to the cultural context of the fourth century Mediterranean world. Discusses the interrelationships between the pagan, Jewish, and Christian communities in Alexandria. ## Full article
### Bibliography
Vrettos, Theodore. _Alexandria: City of the Western Mind_. New York: Free Press, 2001. A lively, fact-filled overview of Alexandrian culture, written by a well-known classicist. Most chapters cover thematic topics, while the first and last discuss the city’s founding and its fall. Includes bibliography, notes, index, and a list of principal figures.

## Full article
**DATE** 332 B.C.E.
**LOCALE** The Nile Delta in Egypt
_The founding of Alexandria created a new city that became a center of Hellenistic culture and learning in North Africa and throughout the Mediterranean._

## Full article
### Key Figures
*   _**Alexander the Great**_ (356- 323 B.C.E.), king of Macedonia, r. 336-323 B.C.E.  
*   _**Ptolemy Soter**_ (367/366- 283/282 B.C.E.), king of Egypt, r. 305-285 B.C.E.  
*   _**Ptolemy Philadelphus**_ (308- 246 B.C.E.), king of Egypt, r. 288-246 B.C.E.  
*   _**Dinocrates**_ (fl. fourth century B.C.E.), architect who planned Alexandria  
*   _**Sostratus of Cnidus**_ (fl. fourth-third century B.C.E.), architect of the lighthouse at Alexandria

## Full article
### Summary of Event
When Alexander the Great took Egypt from the Persians in 332 B.C.E., he had no intention of restoring the country as an independent kingdom. He meant to make it a province of his own, and he believed that a new Hellenic city would make a more suitable capital than one of the old Egyptian towns. This capital was to be named Alexandria in honor of himself as its founder. The site chosen was on the coast, on the western edge of the Nile Delta, where the city would have easy communications with the interior by river and with the outside world by sea. Labor was conscripted from adjacent villages of Egyptian peasants and fishermen, and the work began in 331 B.C.E. with impressive religious ceremonies. Greek seers prophesied that the city would become “large and prosperous, a source of nourishment to many lands.” Construction of the metropolis took years to complete and was still proceeding in the time of Alexander’s successors, Ptolemy Soter and Ptolemy Philadelphus.
The original plan of the city was prepared by the architect Dinocrates, who had it laid out on the grid pattern developed in the fifth century B.C.E. It was divided into four large quarters by two broad avenues. Canopus Street, a processional boulevard 100 feet (30 meters) wide, ran east and west along the long axis; a lesser street running north and south bisected it. At this intersection was the civic center containing the Court of Justice; the Gymnasium, a handsome, colonnaded building whose front stretched 600 feet (183 meters); a series of sacred groves; and, most remarkable of all, an artificial hill dedicated to the god Pan. Its summit could easily be reached by a spiral path, and from this point, visitors—of whom there were many—could survey the entire metropolis.

## Full article
### Summary of Event
The most striking characteristic of Alexandria was its size. By the third century B.C.E., its population had already reached perhaps half a million. By the beginning of the Christian era, it stood at nearly one million, rivaling even the capital of the Roman Empire. One quarter of the city was inhabited by Egyptians and half-caste Greeks, who had no civic rights and performed the menial labor of the city. Another quarter was the residence of the Jews, who came to Egypt in considerable numbers during the reign of Ptolemy Soter. They enjoyed a certain autonomy under their own ethnarch (governor of an ethnic group) and council and constituted one of the most important Jewish settlements in all the ancient world.
The Greco-Macedonian quarter seems to have been near the sea breezes of the waterfront. It is probable that the Europeans were organized into demes and tribes, with an autonomous council and assembly. From east to west along the waterfront stretched warehouses and harbors that received merchant ships from upriver, from Mediterranean ports, and even, via a canal connecting the Nile River with the Red Sea, from the Far East. By the second century B.C.E., there was contact with India, and Buddhist missionaries visited the port. Here, too, were the efficient dockyards of the Ptolemaic navy.
The Royal Quarter was the most imposing of all. It was ornamented with the palaces of the Ptolemies and the nearby monumental tomb of Alexander. Here also was the great Serapeum, a magnificent temple dedicated to the dynasty’s new god, Serapis. The palace complex contained the famous library and museum, where the first two Ptolemies gathered the most distinguished minds of the third century for science and scholarship.
Dominating the skyline and even overshadowing the palace itself was the great stone lighthouse designed by Sostratus of Cnidus. It stood on the island of Pharos, which was connected to the mainland by a manmade mole nearly three-quarters of a mile (a little over a kilometer) long, pierced by two bridged channels for ships. The tower was more than 400 feet (120 meters) high and was provided with a windlass so that firewood could be drawn to the top. Here, fires blazed by night in front of a reflector of polished bronze, warning ships of dangers and guiding them into the harbor.

## Full article
### Summary of Event
In the third century, the culture of Alexandria eclipsed even that of Athens. The scholarship of Aristophanes of Byzantium (c. 257-180 B.C.E.), the astronomy of Aristarchus of Samos (c. 310-c. 230 B.C.E.), the poetry of Callimachus (c. 305-c. 240 B.C.E.), and the medical studies of Erasistratus (c. 304-c. 250 B.C.E.) all were the products of Alexandria. The city was also an important bridge between the cultures of the Greeks and the Jews. The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament, was begun in Alexandria in the third century, and the Jewish scholar Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 B.C.E.-c. 45 C.E.) later worked there.

## The Lighthouse of Alexandria
The Lighthouse of Alexandria, also called the Pharos, was one of the **Seven Wonders of the Ancient World**. It was the only Wonder with a practical, everyday use. It was completed around 280 BC under the Ptolemies. Today its remains lie underwater, near the Citadel of Qaitbay. Scholars have a good idea of its size and shape from ancient descriptions, coins and images.
© Aymantarek24 - Scale Replica of the Lighthouse
Scholars estimate the lighthouse was more than 100 meters (about 330–450 feet) tall. It was built in **three tiers**: the bottom tier was square, the middle tier octagonal and the top tier cylindrical. A ramp led up to the entrance, and a staircase ran up inside.
Little is known about the beacon and the inside of the top two tiers. The lighthouse was damaged by several earthquakes, including one in AD 796, and its upper part had **collapsed** by the Middle Ages. Further earthquakes in the 14th century (notably in 1303 and 1323) left it in ruins. In 1477, Sultan Qaitbay built a fortress on the site, partly using its stones.
Ancient accounts suggest the **beacon** was a large open fire, and some describe a mirror that reflected its light out to sea. The shape of the very top is unclear: ancient records mention a statue, or a pair of statues, standing on top of the lighthouse.
**Underwater excavations** near the site have revealed statues, sphinxes and obelisks that the Ptolemies brought from Heliopolis. Divers have also found colossal statues, about 12 meters (40 feet) tall, of a Ptolemaic king and queen dressed as Egyptian pharaoh and goddess.
In some form, the Lighthouse of Alexandria stood for about 1,600 years.

## The Library of Alexandria
The Library of Alexandria stood in the royal quarter. Ancient writers give very different figures for its size, from about 40,000 up to **700,000 scrolls**. The Ptolemies bought or confiscated books from all over the known world; according to one story, scrolls found on ships in the harbor were copied, and the library kept the originals.
The Ptolemies wanted the library to be the center of knowledge in the Greek world, and many scholars worked there. **Eratosthenes**, its head librarian, calculated the circumference of the Earth. **Euclid** wrote the Elements, the most influential geometry book in history, and Archimedes is said to have studied in Alexandria.
The library **declined** over several centuries rather than vanishing in a single fire. A fire during Julius Caesar's war in Alexandria in 48 BC may have destroyed part of the collection. The Serapeum, a temple of Serapis that served as a "daughter library", was destroyed in AD 391. By the Arab conquest in AD 641, the great library no longer existed.

## The Museum of Ancient Alexandria (Mouseion)
The Mouseion was the research institute of ancient Alexandria, the origin of our word "museum". It was closely linked to the Library and stood in the royal quarter. A mouseion was a **shrine to the Muses**, the nine goddesses who inspired artists, scholars and scientists.
Scholars at the Mouseion studied medicine, philosophy, astronomy and many other subjects, and students were taught there and in the Library. What became of the Mouseion is **unknown**, but its ruins may lie underwater today.

## Other Buildings
### Caesareum
Cleopatra began the Caesareum, a temple probably built in honor of Mark Antony (some sources say Julius Caesar). Augustus completed it and dedicated it to the worship of the **Roman emperors**. Two obelisks, later nicknamed "Cleopatra's Needles", stood in front of it. They were in fact made for Pharaoh Thutmose III, about 1,400 years before Cleopatra, and the Romans moved them to Alexandria from Heliopolis. Today one stands in London and the other in New York.

## Other Buildings
### Cisterns
A network of **underground cisterns** lies beneath Alexandria. Fed by the canal from the Nile, they stored fresh water for the city. The largest have several levels of columns joined by arches. Archaeologists have located many of these cisterns, and a few have been restored.

## Cemeteries
### Catacombs of Kom el-Shaqafa
The **Catacombs** of Kom el-Shaqafa date to the 1st and 2nd centuries AD and were rediscovered in 1900. A spiral staircase around a deep circular shaft leads down several levels. The main burial chamber combines Egyptian, Greek and Roman art and symbols. The catacombs also have many niches for bodies and urns, and a banquet hall where relatives held funeral meals.

## Cemeteries
### The Necropolis (Gabbari)
A rescue dig in the western necropolis at Gabbari revealed more than 17 tombs. **Hundreds** of niches cut into the walls held one or more bodies each, and burial urns stood on the tomb floors. Scholars believe these were the tombs of middle-class Alexandrians.

## Alexandria Today
Alexandria is still a major city. It is Egypt's second-largest city, with more than 5 million inhabitants, and its busiest port. The Arabic name, al-Iskandariyya, still comes from Alexander.
Several places from the ancient city can be visited today:
*   **Citadel of Qaitbay**: the 15th-century fortress built on the site of the Lighthouse.  
*   **Catacombs of Kom el-Shaqafa**: the Roman-era tombs described above.  
*   **Kom el-Dikka**: a Roman theatre, baths and lecture halls in the city center.  
*   **Pompey's Pillar**: a Roman column of red granite, erected in AD 297 in honor of Emperor Diocletian, on the site of the Serapeum.  
*   **Bibliotheca Alexandrina**: a modern library opened in 2002 near the site of the ancient Library, as a tribute to it.

## Frequently Asked Questions About Alexandria
### Who founded Alexandria?
Alexander the Great founded Alexandria in 331 BC.

## Frequently Asked Questions About Alexandria
### Does ancient Alexandria still exist?
The city still exists under the same name, but most of the ancient city lies underneath modern Alexandria or under the sea in the Eastern Harbor.

## Frequently Asked Questions About Alexandria
### Was Alexandria Greek or Egyptian?
Both. Alexandria was a Greek city founded in Egypt, ruled by a Greek-speaking dynasty, with a population of Greeks, Egyptians, Jews and others. Its culture blended Greek and Egyptian traditions.

## Frequently Asked Questions About Alexandria
### Why was Alexandria so important?
Alexandria was the capital of Egypt for almost 1,000 years, a leading trading port of the Mediterranean, and the home of the Lighthouse, one of the Seven Wonders, and the most famous library of the ancient world.

## Alexandria Facts
*   Alexander the Great founded Alexandria in 331 BC.  
*   The Lighthouse of Alexandria (the Pharos), one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, stood in the city's harbor.  
*   The Library and Mouseion of Alexandria were the leading centers of knowledge in the ancient world.

## The Lighthouse of Alexandria
The Lighthouse of Alexandria, also called the Pharos, was one of the **Seven Wonders of the Ancient World**. It was the only Wonder with a practical, everyday use. It was completed around 280 BC under the Ptolemies. Today its remains lie underwater, near the Citadel of Qaitbay. Scholars have a good idea of its size and shape from ancient descriptions, coins and images.
© Aymantarek24 - Scale Replica of the Lighthouse
Scholars estimate the lighthouse was more than 100 meters (about 330–450 feet) tall. It was built in **three tiers**: the bottom tier was square, the middle tier octagonal and the top tier cylindrical. A ramp led up to the entrance, and a staircase ran up inside.
Little is known about the beacon and the inside of the top two tiers. The lighthouse was damaged by several earthquakes, including one in AD 796, and its upper part had **collapsed** by the Middle Ages. Further earthquakes in the 14th century (notably in 1303 and 1323) left it in ruins. In 1477, Sultan Qaitbay built a fortress on the site, partly using its stones.
Ancient accounts suggest the **beacon** was a large open fire, and some describe a mirror that reflected its light out to sea. The shape of the very top is unclear: ancient records mention a statue, or a pair of statues, standing on top of the lighthouse.
**Underwater excavations** near the site have revealed statues, sphinxes and obelisks that the Ptolemies brought from Heliopolis. Divers have also found colossal statues, about 12 meters (40 feet) tall, of a Ptolemaic king and queen dressed as Egyptian pharaoh and goddess.
In some form, the Lighthouse of Alexandria stood for about 1,600 years.
texts.10:
## The Library of Alexandria
The Library of Alexandria stood in the royal quarter. Ancient writers give very different figures for its size, from about 40,000 up to **700,000 scrolls**. The Ptolemies bought or confiscated books from all over the known world; according to one story, scrolls found on ships in the harbor were copied, and the library kept the originals.
The Ptolemies wanted the library to be the center of knowledge in the Greek world, and many scholars worked there. **Eratosthenes**, its head librarian, calculated the circumference of the Earth. **Euclid** wrote the Elements, the most influential geometry book in history, and Archimedes is said to have studied in Alexandria.
The library **declined** over several centuries rather than vanishing in a single fire. A fire during Julius Caesar's war in Alexandria in 48 BC may have destroyed part of the collection. The Serapeum, a temple of Serapis that served as a "daughter library", was destroyed in AD 391. By the Arab conquest in AD 641, the great library no longer existed.
texts.11:
## The Museum of Ancient Alexandria (Mouseion)
The Mouseion was the research institute of ancient Alexandria, the origin of our word "museum". It was closely linked to the Library and stood in the royal quarter. A mouseion was a **shrine to the Muses**, the nine goddesses who inspired artists, scholars and scientists.
Scholars at the Mouseion studied medicine, philosophy, astronomy and many other subjects, and students were taught there and in the Library. What became of the Mouseion is **unknown**, but its ruins may lie underwater today.
texts.12:
## Other Buildings
### Caesareum
Cleopatra began the Caesareum, a temple probably built in honor of Mark Antony (some sources say Julius Caesar). Augustus completed it and dedicated it to the worship of the **Roman emperors**. Two obelisks, later nicknamed "Cleopatra's Needles", stood in front of it. They were in fact made for Pharaoh Thutmose III, about 1,400 years before Cleopatra, and the Romans moved them to Alexandria from Heliopolis. Today one stands in London and the other in New York.
texts.13:
## Other Buildings
### Cisterns
A network of **underground cisterns** lies beneath Alexandria. Fed by the canal from the Nile, they stored fresh water for the city. The largest have several levels of columns joined by arches. Archaeologists have located many of these cisterns, and a few have been restored.
texts.14:
## Cemeteries
### Catacombs of Kom el-Shaqafa
The **Catacombs** of Kom el-Shaqafa date to the 1st and 2nd centuries AD and were rediscovered in 1900. A spiral staircase around a deep circular shaft leads down several levels. The main burial chamber combines Egyptian, Greek and Roman art and symbols. The catacombs also have many niches for bodies and urns, and a banquet hall where relatives held funeral meals.
texts.15:
## Cemeteries
### The Necropolis (Gabbari)
A rescue dig in the western necropolis at Gabbari revealed more than 17 tombs. **Hundreds** of niches cut into the walls held one or more bodies each, and burial urns stood on the tomb floors. Scholars believe these were the tombs of middle-class Alexandrians.
texts.16:
## Alexandria Today
Alexandria is still a major city. It is Egypt's second-largest city, with more than 5 million inhabitants, and its busiest port. The Arabic name, al-Iskandariyya, still comes from Alexander.
Several places from the ancient city can be visited today:
*   **Citadel of Qaitbay**: the 15th-century fortress built on the site of the Lighthouse.  
*   **Catacombs of Kom el-Shaqafa**: the Roman-era tombs described above.  
*   **Kom el-Dikka**: a Roman theatre, baths and lecture halls in the city center.  
*   **Pompey's Pillar**: a Roman column of red granite, erected in AD 297 in honor of Emperor Diocletian, on the site of the Serapeum.  
*   **Bibliotheca Alexandrina**: a modern library opened in 2002 near the site of the ancient Library, as a tribute to it.
texts.17:
## Frequently Asked Questions About Alexandria
### Who founded Alexandria?
Alexander the Great founded Alexandria in 331 BC.
texts.18:
## Frequently Asked Questions About Alexandria
### Does ancient Alexandria still exist?
The city still exists under the same name, but most of the ancient city lies underneath modern Alexandria or under the sea in the Eastern Harbor.
texts.19:
## Frequently Asked Questions About Alexandria
### Was Alexandria Greek or Egyptian?
Both. Alexandria was a Greek city founded in Egypt, ruled by a Greek-speaking dynasty, with a population of Greeks, Egyptians, Jews and others. Its culture blended Greek and Egyptian traditions.
texts.20:
## Frequently Asked Questions About Alexandria
### Why was Alexandria so important?
Alexandria was the capital of Egypt for almost 1,000 years, a leading trading port of the Mediterranean, and the home of the Lighthouse, one of the Seven Wonders, and the most famous library of the ancient world.

### Summary of Event
When Alexander the Great took Egypt from the Persians in 332 B.C.E., he had no intention of restoring the country as an independent kingdom. He meant to make it a province of his own, and he believed that a new Hellenic city would make a more suitable capital than one of the old Egyptian towns. This capital was to be named Alexandria in honor of himself as its founder. The site chosen was on the coast, on the western edge of the Nile Delta, where the city would have easy communications with the interior by river and with the outside world by sea. Labor was conscripted from adjacent villages of Egyptian peasants and fishermen, and the work began in 331 B.C.E. with impressive religious ceremonies. Greek seers prophesied that the city would become “large and prosperous, a source of nourishment to many lands.” Construction of the metropolis took years to complete and was still proceeding in the time of Alexander’s successors, Ptolemy Soter and Ptolemy Philadelphus.
The original plan of the city was prepared by the architect Dinocrates, who had it laid out on the grid pattern developed in the fifth century B.C.E. It was divided into four large quarters by two broad avenues. Canopus Street, a processional boulevard 100 feet (30 meters) wide, ran east and west along the long axis; a lesser street running north and south bisected it. At this intersection was the civic center containing the Court of Justice; the Gymnasium, a handsome, colonnaded building whose front stretched 600 feet (183 meters); a series of sacred groves; and, most remarkable of all, an artificial hill dedicated to the god Pan. Its summit could easily be reached by a spiral path, and from this point, visitors—of whom there were many—could survey the entire metropolis.

## Full article
### Summary of Event
The most striking characteristic of Alexandria was its size. By the third century B.C.E., its population had already reached perhaps half a million. By the beginning of the Christian era, it stood at nearly one million, rivaling even the capital of the Roman Empire. One quarter of the city was inhabited by Egyptians and half-caste Greeks, who had no civic rights and performed the menial labor of the city. Another quarter was the residence of the Jews, who came to Egypt in considerable numbers during the reign of Ptolemy Soter. They enjoyed a certain autonomy under their own ethnarch (governor of an ethnic group) and council and constituted one of the most important Jewish settlements in all the ancient world.
The Greco-Macedonian quarter seems to have been near the sea breezes of the waterfront. It is probable that the Europeans were organized into demes and tribes, with an autonomous council and assembly. From east to west along the waterfront stretched warehouses and harbors that received merchant ships from upriver, from Mediterranean ports, and even, via a canal connecting the Nile River with the Red Sea, from the Far East. By the second century B.C.E., there was contact with India, and Buddhist missionaries visited the port. Here, too, were the efficient dockyards of the Ptolemaic navy.
The Royal Quarter was the most imposing of all. It was ornamented with the palaces of the Ptolemies and the nearby monumental tomb of Alexander. Here also was the great Serapeum, a magnificent temple dedicated to the dynasty’s new god, Serapis. The palace complex contained the famous library and museum, where the first two Ptolemies gathered the most distinguished minds of the third century for science and scholarship.
Dominating the skyline and even overshadowing the palace itself was the great stone lighthouse designed by Sostratus of Cnidus. It stood on the island of Pharos, which was connected to the mainland by a manmade mole nearly three-quarters of a mile (a little over a kilometer) long, pierced by two bridged channels for ships. The tower was more than 400 feet (120 meters) high and was provided with a windlass so that firewood could be drawn to the top. Here, fires blazed by night in front of a reflector of polished bronze, warning ships of dangers and guiding them into the harbor.

### Summary of Event
In the third century, the culture of Alexandria eclipsed even that of Athens. The scholarship of Aristophanes of Byzantium (c. 257-180 B.C.E.), the astronomy of Aristarchus of Samos (c. 310-c. 230 B.C.E.), the poetry of Callimachus (c. 305-c. 240 B.C.E.), and the medical studies of Erasistratus (c. 304-c. 250 B.C.E.) all were the products of Alexandria. The city was also an important bridge between the cultures of the Greeks and the Jews. The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament, was begun in Alexandria in the third century, and the Jewish scholar Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 B.C.E.-c. 45 C.E.) later worked there.

## The Lighthouse of Alexandria
The Lighthouse of Alexandria, also called the Pharos, was one of the **Seven Wonders of the Ancient World**. It was the only Wonder with a practical, everyday use. It was completed around 280 BC under the Ptolemies. Today its remains lie underwater, near the Citadel of Qaitbay. Scholars have a good idea of its size and shape from ancient descriptions, coins and images.
© Aymantarek24 - Scale Replica of the Lighthouse
Scholars estimate the lighthouse was more than 100 meters (about 330–450 feet) tall. It was built in **three tiers**: the bottom tier was square, the middle tier octagonal and the top tier cylindrical. A ramp led up to the entrance, and a staircase ran up inside.
Little is known about the beacon and the inside of the top two tiers. The lighthouse was damaged by several earthquakes, including one in AD 796, and its upper part had **collapsed** by the Middle Ages. Further earthquakes in the 14th century (notably in 1303 and 1323) left it in ruins. In 1477, Sultan Qaitbay built a fortress on the site, partly using its stones.
Ancient accounts suggest the **beacon** was a large open fire, and some describe a mirror that reflected its light out to sea. The shape of the very top is unclear: ancient records mention a statue, or a pair of statues, standing on top of the lighthouse.
**Underwater excavations** near the site have revealed statues, sphinxes and obelisks that the Ptolemies brought from Heliopolis. Divers have also found colossal statues, about 12 meters (40 feet) tall, of a Ptolemaic king and queen dressed as Egyptian pharaoh and goddess.
In some form, the Lighthouse of Alexandria stood for about 1,600 years.

## The Library of Alexandria
The Library of Alexandria stood in the royal quarter. Ancient writers give very different figures for its size, from about 40,000 up to **700,000 scrolls**. The Ptolemies bought or confiscated books from all over the known world; according to one story, scrolls found on ships in the harbor were copied, and the library kept the originals.
The Ptolemies wanted the library to be the center of knowledge in the Greek world, and many scholars worked there. **Eratosthenes**, its head librarian, calculated the circumference of the Earth. **Euclid** wrote the Elements, the most influential geometry book in history, and Archimedes is said to have studied in Alexandria.
The library **declined** over several centuries rather than vanishing in a single fire. A fire during Julius Caesar's war in Alexandria in 48 BC may have destroyed part of the collection. The Serapeum, a temple of Serapis that served as a "daughter library", was destroyed in AD 391. By the Arab conquest in AD 641, the great library no longer existed.

## The Museum of Ancient Alexandria (Mouseion)
The Mouseion was the research institute of ancient Alexandria, the origin of our word "museum". It was closely linked to the Library and stood in the royal quarter. A mouseion was a **shrine to the Muses**, the nine goddesses who inspired artists, scholars and scientists.
Scholars at the Mouseion studied medicine, philosophy, astronomy and many other subjects, and students were taught there and in the Library. What became of the Mouseion is **unknown**, but its ruins may lie underwater today.

## Other Buildings
### Caesareum
Cleopatra began the Caesareum, a temple probably built in honor of Mark Antony (some sources say Julius Caesar). Augustus completed it and dedicated it to the worship of the **Roman emperors**. Two obelisks, later nicknamed "Cleopatra's Needles", stood in front of it. They were in fact made for Pharaoh Thutmose III, about 1,400 years before Cleopatra, and the Romans moved them to Alexandria from Heliopolis. Today one stands in London and the other in New York.

## Other Buildings
### Cisterns
A network of **underground cisterns** lies beneath Alexandria. Fed by the canal from the Nile, they stored fresh water for the city. The largest have several levels of columns joined by arches. Archaeologists have located many of these cisterns, and a few have been restored.

## Cemeteries
### Catacombs of Kom el-Shaqafa
The **Catacombs** of Kom el-Shaqafa date to the 1st and 2nd centuries AD and were rediscovered in 1900. A spiral staircase around a deep circular shaft leads down several levels. The main burial chamber combines Egyptian, Greek and Roman art and symbols. The catacombs also have many niches for bodies and urns, and a banquet hall where relatives held funeral meals.

## Cemeteries
### The Necropolis (Gabbari)
A rescue dig in the western necropolis at Gabbari revealed more than 17 tombs. **Hundreds** of niches cut into the walls held one or more bodies each, and burial urns stood on the tomb floors. Scholars believe these were the tombs of middle-class Alexandrians.

## Alexandria Today
Alexandria is still a major city. It is Egypt's second-largest city, with more than 5 million inhabitants, and its busiest port. The Arabic name, al-Iskandariyya, still comes from Alexander.
Several places from the ancient city can be visited today:
*   **Citadel of Qaitbay**: the 15th-century fortress built on the site of the Lighthouse.  
*   **Catacombs of Kom el-Shaqafa**: the Roman-era tombs described above.  
*   **Kom el-Dikka**: a Roman theatre, baths and lecture halls in the city center.  
*   **Pompey's Pillar**: a Roman column of red granite, erected in AD 297 in honor of Emperor Diocletian, on the site of the Serapeum.  
*   **Bibliotheca Alexandrina**: a modern library opened in 2002 near the site of the ancient Library, as a tribute to it.

## Frequently Asked Questions About Alexandria
### Who founded Alexandria?
Alexander the Great founded Alexandria in 331 BC.

## Frequently Asked Questions About Alexandria
### Does ancient Alexandria still exist?
The city still exists under the same name, but most of the ancient city lies underneath modern Alexandria or under the sea in the Eastern Harbor.

## Frequently Asked Questions About Alexandria
### Was Alexandria Greek or Egyptian?
Both. Alexandria was a Greek city founded in Egypt, ruled by a Greek-speaking dynasty, with a population of Greeks, Egyptians, Jews and others. Its culture blended Greek and Egyptian traditions.

## Frequently Asked Questions About Alexandria
### Why was Alexandria so important?
Alexandria was the capital of Egypt for almost 1,000 years, a leading trading port of the Mediterranean, and the home of the Lighthouse, one of the Seven Wonders, and the most famous library of the ancient world.

## Alexandria Facts
*   Alexander the Great founded Alexandria in 331 BC.  
*   The Lighthouse of Alexandria (the Pharos), one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, stood in the city's harbor.  
*   The Library and Mouseion of Alexandria were the leading centers of knowledge in the ancient world.  
*   The Ptolemies ruled Egypt from Alexandria for almost 300 years.  
*   Alexander the Great was buried in Alexandria, but archaeologists have not yet found his tomb.  
*   The remains of the Lighthouse and the royal quarter now lie underwater.  
*   People from Alexandria are called Alexandrians.  
*   Archaeologists are uncovering more about ancient Alexandria every year.

When Alexander the Great took Egypt from the Persians in 332 B.C.E., he had no intention of restoring the country as an independent kingdom. This capital was to be named Alexandria in honor of himself as its founder. The site chosen was on the coast, on the western edge of the Nile Delta, where the city would have easy communications with the interior by river and with the outside world by sea. Labor was conscripted from adjacent villages of Egyptian peasants and fishermen, and the work began in 331 B.C.E. with impressive religious ceremonies. Greek seers prophesied that the city would become “large and prosperous, a source of nourishment to many lands.” Construction of the metropolis took years to complete and was still proceeding in the time of Alexander’s successors, Ptolemy Soter and Ptolemy Philadelphus.
The original plan of the city was prepared by the architect Dinocrates, who had it laid out on the grid pattern developed in the fifth century B.C.E. It was divided into four large quarters by two broad avenues. Canopus Street, a processional boulevard 100 feet (30 meters) wide, ran east and west along the long axis; a lesser street running north and south bisected it. At this intersection was the civic center containing the Court of Justice; the Gymnasium, a handsome, colonnaded building whose front stretched 600 feet (183 meters); a series of sacred groves; and, most remarkable of all, an artificial hill dedicated to the god Pan. The most striking characteristic of Alexandria was its size. By the third century B.C.E., its population had already reached perhaps half a million. By the beginning of the Christian era, it stood at nearly one million, rivaling even the capital of the Roman Empire. One quarter of the city was inhabited by Egyptians and half-caste Greeks, who had no civic rights and performed the menial labor of the city. Another quarter was the residence of the Jews, who came to Egypt in considerable numbers during the reign of Ptolemy Soter. They enjoyed a certain autonomy under their own ethnarch (governor of an ethnic group) and council and constituted one of the most important Jewish settlements in all the ancient world.
The Greco-Macedonian quarter seems to have been near the sea breezes of the waterfront. From east to west along the waterfront stretched warehouses and harbors that received merchant ships from upriver, from Mediterranean ports, and even, via a canal connecting the Nile River with the Red Sea, from the Far East. By the second century B.C.E., there was contact with India, and Buddhist missionaries visited the port. Here, too, were the efficient dockyards of the Ptolemaic navy.
The Royal Quarter was the most imposing of all. It was ornamented with the palaces of the Ptolemies and the nearby monumental tomb of Alexander. Here also was the great Serapeum, a magnificent temple dedicated to the dynasty’s new god, Serapis. The palace complex contained the famous library and museum, where the first two Ptolemies gathered the most distinguished minds of the third century for science and scholarship.
Dominating the skyline and even overshadowing the palace itself was the great stone lighthouse designed by Sostratus of Cnidus. It stood on the island of Pharos, which was connected to the mainland by a manmade mole nearly three-quarters of a mile (a little over a kilometer) long, pierced by two bridged channels for ships. The tower was more than 400 feet (120 meters) high and was provided with a windlass so that firewood could be drawn to the top.
